source: NYSED guide for suicide prevention for school personnel
topic: who carries out the risk assessment
text: A suicide risk assessment is carried out by a member of the school crisis team who has been trained for it. Where possible, two team members interview the student together. The C-SSRS is suggested as the screening tool, and ongoing staff training in assessment, safety planning and referral is recommended.

source: NYSED guide for suicide prevention for school personnel
topic: supervision when a student may be at risk
text: A student who may be at risk is not left alone at any point, including trips to the restroom, and is not allowed to leave school or take the bus home. Supervision continues until a caregiver who can stay with them takes over. If the student goes to hospital, a staff member stays until a parent or guardian arrives.

source: Pasadena USD: When a student expresses suicidal thoughts at school
topic: first response by staff
text: Staff who are not counsellors or administrators stay with the student while someone fetches a counsellor, school psychologist or administrator immediately. The student is moved to a secure place away from other students where they can be monitored. The risk level is assessed by a counsellor, psychologist or administrator, not by the staff member who received the disclosure.

source: NYSED guide for suicide prevention for school personnel
topic: means restriction
text: Any means of self-harm the student has access to are removed, and the student is told what is being done at each step. When the parent or guardian is contacted, the school stresses securing firearms, medications and other dangerous items at home.

source: NYSED guide for suicide prevention for school personnel
topic: notifying the parent or guardian
text: Parents or guardians are contacted immediately whenever suicidal signs appear or a risk assessment is carried out. Where emergency services have not been called, they are asked to come to the school. The school explains the reasons for concern and the follow-up options. Child protective services are contacted if abuse or neglect is suspected, or if a parent will not keep the child safe.

source: NYSED guide for suicide prevention for school personnel
topic: safety planning
text: A written safety plan is developed with the student and their parent or guardian by a trained team member, ideally a mental health professional. It records warning signs, coping strategies the student can use, people who can offer support, and a crisis line or text line. Means restriction forms part of the plan.

source: Pasadena USD: When a student expresses suicidal thoughts at school
topic: reviewing and sharing the safety plan
text: The safety plan is made together with the student or their medical provider, and is reviewed periodically rather than written once. Teachers and staff who need to know are informed of causes, warning signs and coping strategies, and the parent or guardian is told the plan is in place.

source: NYSED guide for suicide prevention for school personnel
topic: referral and consent to share information
text: The student is referred to community services or a mental health professional for follow-up care, and the options include 24-hour support, since suicidal thinking does not keep to school hours. Schools help families make appointments and obtain signed consent so that school staff and the student's providers can speak to each other.

source: NYSED guide for suicide prevention for school personnel
topic: documentation
text: Every step of the assessment and the response is documented, along with all contact with parents or guardians, so that it is clear the protocol was followed. Student information is shared only with those who need to know.

source: NYSED guide for suicide prevention for school personnel
topic: follow-up timing and return to school
text: Follow-up is set at one week, or sooner if the safety plan says so, and again at one month. Before a student returns after an attempt or a hospital stay, a return-to-school meeting is planned, because the risk of a further attempt is higher in this period.

source: School Mental Health Ontario: Talking with students about suicide
topic: asking about suicide directly
text: There is no evidence that asking about suicide or discussing it carefully raises risk. A careful conversation can show care, reduce stigma and make it easier for a student to ask for help. Staff are advised to use plain, concrete language and to avoid phrasing that implies blame, such as "committed suicide".

source: School Mental Health Ontario: Talking with students about suicide
topic: the limits of a staff member's role
text: School staff are not expected to assess suicide risk or manage a disclosure alone. Their role is to notice concerns, listen without judgement, follow the board's protocol and connect the student to support immediately. A student who has indicated suicidal intent is never left alone.

source: School Mental Health Ontario: Talking with students about suicide
topic: what to avoid in the conversation
text: Conversations avoid discussing methods and graphic detail, and staff do not share their own experiences of suicide. Suicide is not presented as a way to solve problems, and simple single-cause explanations are avoided. Students are pointed towards credible supports and cautioned against relying on non-credible sources such as social media or artificial intelligence.

source: School Mental Health Ontario: Talking with students about suicide
topic: describing available supports
text: Students are told about supports in school and in the community by name rather than in general: staff who can help, local child and youth mental health services, and 24/7 crisis lines. Help-seeking is framed as a skill that improves with practice, and it may take more than one attempt to find the right fit.

source: AFSP: Suicide prevention in K-12 schools
topic: staff training and school policy
text: Schools should have comprehensive prevention, intervention and postvention policies, and staff who interact with students should receive regular suicide-prevention training so they can recognise risk and refer on. Students should also be taught to recognise warning signs in themselves or their peers and to seek help.

source: JED Foundation: Faculty guide to supporting student mental health
topic: noticing that a student may be struggling
text: Early signs that a student is struggling include missed assignments, repeated absences, falling grades and less participation than usual. Visible changes such as marked fatigue or a decline in personal care may also be apparent, as may distressing content in submitted work. These are reasons to check in with the student, not conclusions about their mental health.

source: JED Foundation: Faculty guide to supporting student mental health
topic: opening a check-in conversation
text: A check-in is best held privately, for example after class or in an office. The staff member describes what they have observed and then asks open questions about how the student is doing. The guidance is to lean towards checking in, on the view that an unnecessary conversation costs far less than overlooking a student who is struggling.

source: JED Foundation: Faculty guide to supporting student mental health
topic: responding when a student describes a difficulty
text: When a student describes a difficulty, the response is to acknowledge what they have said and offer to help them find support. Confidentiality is not promised, because some concerns must be passed on. The staff member's role is to notice, listen and connect the student with help, not to act as a mental health professional.

source: JED Foundation: Faculty guide to supporting student mental health
topic: knowing which campus services exist
text: Staff are advised to establish with student affairs or the dean of students which services the institution actually provides, such as counseling, a behavioral intervention or care team, health services, academic support and disability services, so that a referral names a real service rather than a general suggestion. Listing these in course materials, alongside 24-hour crisis options, puts them in front of students before anyone needs them.

source: PHQ-9 scoring and proposed treatment actions (Kroenke, Spitzer and Williams)
topic: what the PHQ-9 score suggests outside a crisis
text: The severity bands published with the PHQ-9 are paired with proposed actions. A total of 5 to 9 is treated as mild and matched with watchful waiting and repeating the questionnaire at follow-up. A total of 10 to 14 is treated as moderate, where a treatment plan is to be considered, including counseling and follow-up. These are suggested actions for a clinician to weigh, not automatic decisions.
